lead: Offshore the chart is small in scale and nobody checks the plot but you. Know what the projection does to distance, what each publication gives, and how far to trust the plotter.

sections.title: What the projection does to distance and course

qa.q: How do I measure distance correctly on a Mercator chart?
qa.a: On the **latitude scale** level with the leg: Mercator scale grows towards the pole as the secant of the latitude, so the scale in the chart's title holds only at the latitude it names.

refs: Charts — Mercator projection
Charts — distance on the latitude scale
Charts — gnomonic charts and great circles

blocks.p: On a **Mercator** chart a straight line is a rhumb line: one true course throughout. The price is scale, which grows towards the pole as the secant of the latitude. Measure distance on the latitude scale level with the leg; the scale in the title holds only at the latitude it names.

fig.note: Mercator: the same 600 M takes more paper further north

fig.title: Scale by latitude: worked example
lines: Leg at 48°N read on the scale at 42°N: 50.0'

blocks.p: A **great circle** is a straight line on a **gnomonic** chart, but that chart keeps no angles. Take points off the line every 5° of longitude, plot them on the Mercator and sail rhumb lines between them. Over a few hundred miles it saves almost nothing.

sections.title: Course and distance by calculation

qa.q: How do I calculate course and distance between two positions without plotting them?
qa.a: By **Mercator sailing**: tan course = d.long ÷ the difference of meridional parts, and distance = d.lat ÷ cos course. To work a position forward, use mid-latitude sailing, with departure = d.long × cos latitude.

refs: Charts — latitude and longitude
Charts — latitude and longitude — mid-latitude sailing
Charts — Mercator projection — Mercator sailing

blocks.p: A minute of latitude is a mile; a minute of longitude is a mile only on the equator. East–west miles are **departure**: d.long × cos latitude. Decimals of a degree are not minutes: 0.25° is 15.0'. On a chart too small to plot on, work the position by **mid-latitude sailing**, or a long leg by **Mercator sailing**.

sections.title: How much a millimetre is worth

qa.q: Which chart should I plot on when two charts of the same area disagree?
qa.a: On the **largest-scale** chart that covers the leg: where two charts differ, believe the larger scale. Offshore, carry the plot onto the next chart by latitude and longitude.

blocks.p: Plot on the largest-scale chart that covers the leg; where two charts differ, believe the larger scale. The **folio** holds, on paper, the passage chart and the approaches and plans of the destination, every port of refuge and any pilotage on the way. Offshore, carry the plot onto the next chart by latitude and longitude.

fig.note: Six hours of EP can be out by more than 0.9 M

blocks.p: A **horizontal datum** shift of 0.08' is 150 m: invisible on the passage chart, 6 mm on a 1:25,000 approach. An old plan sounded to MLWS shows more water than one reduced to LAT. Read the units: 7₃ on a fathoms chart is 7 fathoms 3 feet, 13.7 m.

sections.title: Instruments, bearings, speed and time

qa.q: How do I convert a true course to magnetic?
qa.a: Add westerly **variation**, subtract easterly: 205°T with 6°W variation is 211°M. Set the variation on a Breton plotter and it is applied for you.

blocks.p: A **Breton plotter** needs only a meridian or parallel under its grid, never the table's edge; its arrow points the way you go, or you read the reciprocal. Creeping dividers and a bowed plotter falsify every leg: 3° over 60 M is 3 M. Plot lightly in soft pencil. Take hand bearings where a transit has proved the compass.
True to magnetic: add westerly variation, subtract easterly. Set on the plotter, it is applied for you. Light sectors are true, from seaward: convert your bearing first.

sections.title: Routes, installations and areas

qa.q: How close can a yacht go to an oil platform or rig?
qa.a: No closer than its **500 m safety zone**, which rigs and single buoy moorings have too. In fog a platform sounds Mo(U), heard about 2 M off.

blocks.p: In fog a platform sounds Mo(U), heard about 2 M off. A **wind farm** has national rules in its chart note: who may transit, and when. Check the blade-tip height against your mast; never anchor among its cables. A fouled cable is slipped, buoyed and reported. An ODAS data buoy is a yellow special mark, Fl(5) Y 20s. A light buoy replacing a lightvessel has a fraction of its range.

sections.title: What to open, and how to keep it current

qa.q: How far away will I see a lighthouse at night?
qa.a: At the lesser of two ranges: the **geographical range**, 2.08 × (√H + √h) miles for heights in metres, and the luminous range, the nominal range cut down by tonight's visibility.

sections.title: Settings that make the plotter worth trusting

qa.q: How do I set the safety contour on my chart plotter?
qa.a: **Safety contour** = draught + squat + half the swell + margin; the plotter then bolds the next deeper contour in the cell. Only an ENC can sound the alarm, not an RNC, which is a picture of the paper chart.

blocks.p: An **RNC** is a picture of the paper chart; an **ENC** is data, so only an ENC can sound an alarm, about what you set and what its cells hold.

blocks.p: A contour at the bare draught misses a shoal the troughs uncover; a factory 30 m alarm cries wolf. A leg with no cell is unchecked; the 'Basic' display hides soundings. **Overscale**: the cell's error, about 0.5 mm at its compilation scale, grows with the zoom: buy the approach cells. At speed, zoom out to see minutes ahead. A plot copied from the plotter checks nothing: keep a DR, cross-check by bearings, depth or radar. No alarm replaces the lookout.
